talks.title: Attacking SCCM with SCCMHunter | Garrett Foster
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Attacking SCCM with SCCMHunter | Garrett Foster.
talks.summary:
Overview: Garrett Foster of SpecterOps presents at Wild West Hackin' Fest on attacking Microsoft SCCM using the SCCMHunter toolset.

Key Topics: SCCM architecture and excessive enterprise trust in endpoint management; community research on SCCM attack paths; distribution point discovery via WDS service connection points; and BloodHound graph integration.

Technical Details: Foster demonstrates identifying SCCM distribution points by querying Active Directory for WDS service connection point child objects. SCCMHunter automates enumeration and exploitation of SCCM misconfigurations.

Takeaways: Endpoint management platforms like SCCM represent high-trust infrastructure that attackers actively target. Red and blue teams should assess SCCM configurations and monitor for unauthorized queries.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Announcements & Evolving ROADtools for Entra ID Recon & Tokens | Dirk-jan Mollema.
talks.summary:
ROADtools Overview

Dirk-jan Mollema presents ROADtools for Microsoft Entra ID enumeration and token operations. Released in 2020, the open-source toolkit centers on ROADlib authentication flows, ROADrecon for tenant reconnaissance, and ROADtx for token exchange.

Red and Blue Team Utility

ROADrecon runs from low-privilege accounts to enumerate tenant data useful for both red-team mapping and blue-team analysis when the Azure portal hides relationships. ROADtx handles refresh tokens, access tokens, cookies, and memory-extracted credentials.

Azure AD Graph Deprecation

The tool relies on graph.windows.net's Azure AD Graph API, including an internal version exposing conditional access policies without privileged roles. Microsoft is deprecating this API in favor of the more restricted Microsoft Graph, which limits visibility into internal Entra properties.

Privilege Analysis Demo

Mollema previews detecting hidden global-admin privileges through user "Bob," demonstrating how ROADrecon analysis surfaces authorization paths not obvious in standard portal views.

talks.title: Breaking Entra: Identity Attacks You Can Recreate | Jonathan Elkabas
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Breaking Entra: Identity Attacks You Can Recreate | Jonathan Elkabas.
talks.summary:
Identity Is Not the Whole Perimeter

Jonathan Elkabas argues “identity is the new perimeter” understates the problem: buying credentials bypasses technical controls, and non-human identities dominate modern tenants. Microsoft reports far more workload identities than human users, many over-permissioned.

Entra Identity Sprawl

He breaks down service principals behind enterprise apps, system- and user-assigned managed identities for Azure resources, and newer agent identities tied to Copilot and AI services—calling the overlapping terminology organized confusion attackers exploit.

Midnight Blizzard Case Study

The talk revisits APT29’s Microsoft breach starting from password spray against a legacy test tenant and escalating to executive email access, illustrating how minor misconfigurations chain into tenant compromise.

Entra Goat Lab

Elkabas introduces Entra Goat, a deliberately vulnerable Entra ID environment for safely practicing attack paths end to end. The session demos misconfiguration chains attackers use in the wild and encourages hands-on recreation in isolated labs.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in MQL for Email APT Hunting | Bryan Campbell.
talks.summary:
Platform overview

Brian Campbell of Sublime explains MQL (Message Query Language) for email threat hunting, supported by Autonomous Security Analyst and Autonomous Detection Engineer components for adaptive defense.

MQL and enrichments

MQL expresses attacker TTPs with organizational context, NLU, computer vision, OCR, link rendering, WHOIS, ML scoring, and deep attachment analysis via File Explode/Strelka across nested archives, macros, HTML smuggling, and encrypted zips.

Risk scoring

Multiple weak signals are weighted into one interpretable severity score to reduce false positives and catch sophisticated campaigns that evade single-indicator rules.

APT29 example

He details Russian espionage email tradecraft—thread hijacking, secure-document lures, OAuth consent abuse, and inbox-rule forwarding—and walks through a diplomatic spearphish using HTML smuggling to drop IMG/ISO/LNK/DLL chains designed to bypass attachment-only controls, with MQL focused on detecting the HTML dropper.

talks.title: From Lure to Alert: Implementing Canary Tokens in M365 | Ryan O'Donnell
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding From Lure to Alert: Implementing Canary Tokens in M365 | Ryan O'Donnell.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Ryan O'Donnell describes piloting mailbox-based canary tokens in Microsoft 365 using native audit telemetry rather than third-party tripwires.

## Motivation and Threat Model
After initial cloud compromise, actors like Storm 2372 run crude keyword searches—"password," "admin," credentials—across stolen mailboxes. O'Donnell targets this predictable post-compromise behavior to shrink dwell time below industry medians.

## Implementation Details
Lure emails are planted in hidden folders such as Recoverable Items, which remain searchable even when not visible in the UI. Testing with Graphrunner confirmed keyword searches surface canary content. Day 12 of the first pilot produced an alert at 11:47 p.m. based solely on mailbox operations—no EDR or malware signals.

## Takeaways
M365-native canary tokens can detect intruder mailbox reconnaissance early, but require careful lure placement, tuning, and validation that hidden folders remain indexed.

talks.title: I'm In Your Logs Now, Deceiving Your Analysts and Blinding Your EDR | Olaf Hartong
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in I'm In Your Logs Now, Deceiving Your Analysts and Blinding Your EDR | Olaf Hartong.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Olaf Hartong demonstrates how Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)—an operating system facility designed originally for performance monitoring and debugging rather than security—can be manipulated to deceive security analysts, forge alerts, and blind Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents. Because security tools such as Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike, and Elastic rely extensively on ETW for visibility beyond standard kernel callbacks, fundamental architectural traits of ETW create exploitable weaknesses that allow unprivileged or low-privileged actors to spoof telemetry or exhaust logging capacities.

### Key Topics
- **ETW Architecture and Security Products**: ETW connects providers (applications or drivers generating events), session controllers/the ETW kernel, and consumers (such as EDR agents). EDR vendors prefer ETW for stability (avoiding crash-prone kernel drivers), granular filtering, dynamic configuration, and broad coverage across hundreds of providers.
- **Event Spoofing Without Elevation**: ETW allows any user-mode process to call `EventRegister` with a provider's GUID and emit events using `EventWrite`. While ETW attaches the authentic originating Process ID (preventing PID spoofing), it does not track which process registered or emitted the event, enabling attackers to inject arbitrary synthetic logs.
- **Abusing Ingestion Caps to Blind Sensors**: Cloud-connected EDRs implement event capping to manage costs, performance, and bandwidth. Hartong discovered that by generating synthetic queries (such as random LDAP lookups) until hitting local or global 24-hour caps (e.g., 1,000 events), real offensive actions (such as SharpHound or AD Explorer activity) are completely dropped from telemetry.
- **Buffer Exhaustion**: Trace sessions use kernel non-paged memory buffer pools. By launching an unconsumed trace session with maximum pool configurations and flooding events, the ETW kernel tells providers that buffers are full, dropping telemetry across all concurrent sessions listening to that provider—including the EDR.

### Technical Details
- **Permissions and Registration**: ETW access control primarily protects event consumption via Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL) strings, leaving event emission largely unrestricted. Users in the `PerformanceLogUsers` group (which non-elevated accounts are often added to, such as when Visual Studio is installed) gain broad tracing rights.
- **Telemetry Injection Nuances**: Writing custom events required accounting for Windows little-endian byte ordering and specific event header structures that off-the-shelf consumer-focused packages omitted. Using these techniques, Hartong was able to forge LDAP queries, AMSI events, and fake antivirus/ransomware detections.
- **Tooling Released**: Hartong developed research utilities including *ProvMon* (to monitor provider registrations) and *Bamboozle EDR* (to automate event spoofing, telemetry flooding, and trace buffer exhaustion).
- **Vendor Response**: After reporting to Microsoft, initial remediations only addressed the specific ransomware detection proof of concept and introduced signature detections against the POC binary, leaving the core architectural issues and 98+ other providers unpatched.

### Takeaways
- **Defensive Blind Trust**: Security analysts must recognize that endpoint logs and SIEM data derived from ETW cannot be inherently trusted as immutable, ground truth evidence.
- **Detection Opportunities**: Defenders can monitor for abnormal telemetry patterns—such as rapid volumetric spikes followed by total silence in specific log tables—or attempt provider registration monitoring (though registration logging is inherently noisy).
- **Architectural Resolution**: Because event emission abuse and buffer suppression stem from kernel-level design choices within ETW, full remediation requires deep architectural adjustments by Microsoft rather than superficial signature blocks.

talks.title: # ClickForClickOnce - Generate Configurable Clickonce Payloads | Debjeet Banerjee
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding # ClickForClickOnce - Generate Configurable Clickonce Payloads | Debjeet Banerjee.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Tool Shed presentation, Debjeet Banerjee ("DB"), a malware developer for Black Hills Information Security (BHIS), introduces **ClickForClickOnce**, an open-source framework designed to automate the creation of configurable Microsoft ClickOnce payloads for penetration testing and red teaming. Historically, ClickOnce was used by organizations to distribute self-updating Windows applications with minimal user interaction via a link. For red teams, it offers an effective initial access vector requiring just two user clicks (Open and Run), leaves no artifacts in standard browser download directories, avoids SmartScreen blocks typically seen on EXEs or DLLs, and experiences comparatively fewer detections. However, manual ClickOnce payload creation via Visual Studio on Windows is time-consuming and difficult to automate under engagement deadlines. ClickForClickOnce solves this by offering an automated web interface packaged via Docker.

### Key Topics
- **Architecture and Interface:** ClickForClickOnce runs in a Docker container using a Caddy web server (serving static content and zipping artifacts) and a FastAPI backend to handle build configurations. A simple web UI allows operators to build customized payloads without wrestling with complex tool setup or dependencies.
- **Configurable Payload Options:** 
  - *Naming:* Tailoring the application display name (e.g., matching a target organization's IT tooling) to make execution prompts believable.
  - *Size Inflation:* Artificially inflating file size (typically to 200–300 MB) to bypass or delay immediate EDR scanning. The tool inflates the text section up to ~10 MB (to avoid excessive entropy spikes) and appends random data in resource files for the remainder.
  - *AppDomain Injection:* Running payloads under Microsoft-signed binaries (such as TzSync, PowerShell ISE, ServiceHub, or powershell.exe) to execute shellcode without forced DLL injection.
  - *Configurable Actions:* Chaining actions including shellcode execution (configurable in `program.cs`, with a default 8-minute delay to counter EDR inspection of read-write-execute memory allocations), dropping files to disk, and executing OS commands (supporting environment variables).

### Technical Details & EDR Detections
- **Execution Chain:** Delivering a `.application` file prompts the user to open and run it. The browser invokes Windows ClickOnce handler `dfsvc.exe`.
- **EDR Test Results:** Field testing showed strong success with zero detections against Microsoft Defender (MD), SentinelOne, and Sophos. In contrast, CrowdStrike Falcon and Cylance regularly detect the process. The speaker highlighted that detections are rarely triggered by the payload itself; rather, `dfsvc.exe` triggers a call to `rundll32.exe`, which EDRs flag or block outright before shell execution. When shells are established, subsequent beacons are sometimes blocked due to network indicators. Banerjee observed that post-CrowdStrike-outage shifts have pushed EDR focus heavily toward network behavior, domain fronting, and URL/CDN reputation (such as burned Dev Tunnels).
- **Browser & Formats:** While modern browsers handle `.application` files, older browsers can utilize `.appref-ms` files, which can also be embedded in documents.

### Takeaways & Defensive Considerations
- **Detection Strategies:** Defenders can identify malicious ClickOnce usage by detecting signed binaries (like `powershell_ise.exe`) executing from user AppData directories instead of `System32`. Monitoring for `.exe.config` files associated with AppDomain injection, unusual DLL sideloads, and unexpected `dfsvc.exe` spawning of `rundll32.exe` provides reliable detection opportunities.
- **Application Allowlisting:** Although AppLocker can challenge ClickOnce execution, operators can bypass restrictions by using generated artifacts (`.exe.config` and payload DLLs) combined with environment variables to force AppDomain injection when whitelisted executables launch.

talks.title: Elicitation: Weaponizing Social Engineering for Covert Access Operations | Dorota Kozlowska
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Elicitation: Weaponizing Social Engineering for Covert Access Operations | Dorota Kozlowska.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Dorota Kozlowska, a penetration tester with Black Hills Information Security (BHIS) working in the Anti-SoC continuous penetration testing team and a Certified Covert Access Specialist, presents on using social engineering elicitation during covert access operations. The presentation explores how physical penetration testing integrates with social engineering to expose vulnerabilities in physical security controls (such as locks, barriers, cameras, and guards) and human procedures. Kozlowska emphasizes that elicitation leverages human psychology—including the desire to be helpful, ego, and the instinct to correct errors—to subtly extract sensitive data without raising suspicion.

### Key Topics
- **Physical Penetration Testing Fundamentals:** Kozlowska underscores the necessity of having a documented scope and a "get out of jail free card" signed by leadership before entering a target facility. Working in pairs allows teams to stage distractions (e.g., dropping documents in a bank lobby to draw eyes away from turnstiles). Testers must discreetly document their findings through approved photo or video capture while respecting agreed-upon rules of engagement.
- **Phases of Social Engineering:** Kozlowska outlines the attack lifecycle across reconnaissance, engagement, exploitation, and execution. Reconnaissance involves gathering intelligence on employee names, roles, shift habits, org charts, and floor plans. Engagement focuses on rapport-building and establishing plausible pretexts. Exploitation involves influencing targets to breach normal processes or reveal restricted data, leading to the execution phase where objectives (such as accessing a server room or placing a flag) are achieved.
- **Psychological Foundations of Elicitation:** Elicitation differs from direct interrogation; it feels like casual conversation. Attackers exploit psychological principles such as reciprocity, social proof, perceived authority, sympathy for a confused individual, and foot-in-the-door consistency.

### Technical Details
- **Elicitation and Framing Techniques:** Operators utilize subtle challenges, innocent inquiries, and false information testing (deliberately offering inaccurate claims so targets instinctively correct them to defend accuracy). Framing techniques shape how inquiries are perceived:
  - *Praise & Ego Framing:* Complimenting a target's expertise so they reveal proprietary system architectures.
  - *Challenge Framing:* Provoking detailed technical explanations by expressing doubt that a system works a certain way.
  - *Sympathy / Helpless Persona:* Posing as a confused new hire or contractor struggling with access.
  - *Presumed Familiarity & Third-Party Framing:* Dropping internal tool names, Active Directory groups, or colleague names to validate procedures without formal requests.
- **Mirroring and Active Listening:** Replicating a target's tone, pacing, posture, and language creates rapport and encourages unguarded venting or disclosure of operational workarounds.
- **Technical Access Mapping:** Kozlowska demonstrates how an attacker can incrementally map an enterprise access path without triggering helpdesk alerts—such as chatting with IT support to confirm VPN clients (e.g., AnyConnect vs. Fortinet), confirming Active Directory group naming conventions with HR, and checking MFA trust models (e.g., Duo vs. Okta) with developers.

### Takeaways
- **Operational Tradecraft:** Operators should maintain confidence, stick strictly to timelines, avoid lingering unnecessarily, retain plausible backstories, and remove all physical equipment during exit.
- **Defensive Strategies & Awareness:** Organizations must train employees that casual inquiries can be weaponized. Red flags include subtle testing of procedures, repeated rephrased questions, excessive flattery, and artificial urgency. Defensive responses include deflecting, refusing to over-explain or educate, answering with clarifying questions, generalizing responses, adhering strictly to workplace rules, and reporting suspicious encounters quietly.
- **Ethics & Continuous Testing:** Elicitation must adhere to ethical boundaries and legal frameworks (such as the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, GDPR, and wire fraud laws). Continuous red-team-inspired testing is vital as technologies and communication mediums evolve.

talks.title: Strengthening Cybersecurity Potential: Investing in People Instead of Tools! | Markus Schober
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Strengthening Cybersecurity Potential: Investing in People Instead of Tools! | Markus Schober.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Markus Schober, founder of Blue Cape Security and former principal consultant at IBM X-Force, argues that strengthening cybersecurity resilience requires prioritizing investments in people rather than continually purchasing new tooling. While leadership often leans toward capital expense investments in point solutions, tools without skilled operators lead to underutilization, alert fatigue, and critical detection gaps. Schober presents a practical blueprint for developing structured onboarding, hands-on training, and career advancement paths to improve retention, operational efficiency, and overall security capabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Tool-First Mindset vs. Foundational Competency**: Security tools provide an abstracted layer that lacks human context and critical thinking. Relying solely on tool outputs without understanding underlying fundamentals causes analysts to misinterpret alerts or overlook real intrusions.
- **The SOC Fatigue and Turnover Crisis**: Referencing data from a Tines report ("Voice of the SOC Analyst"), Schober highlights that 71% of analysts experience burnout, 64% spend over half their time on tedious manual tasks, and 64% consider switching jobs within a year. Repetitive, shallow triage with unclear development paths drives talent drain.
- **Underutilization and Maintenance Overhead**: Organizations often operate tools at only a fraction of their capability because analysts are not trained to tune them. Furthermore, managing and maintaining automation and point solutions requires significant ongoing human resources.
- **Real-World Breach Lessons**: Schober reviews a CISA advisory where an agency suffered a multi-week intrusion due to ignored EDR alerts, unpatched vulnerabilities, and an unexercised incident response plan that failed to provide third-party responders with necessary access. In another instance, an outsourced MDR team dismissed valid ransomware alerts running from `AppData\Local\Temp` as false positives due to a lack of basic technical knowledge, leading to an entire enterprise network being shut down.

### Technical Details & Training Roadmap
To illustrate transforming a security team from basic triage to advanced capabilities, Schober outlines a multi-year "Crawl, Walk, Run" maturity framework:
- **Foundations (Crawl)**: Focuses on core enterprise architecture, including Windows domains, domain admin/service accounts, authentication event analysis, credential attacks, and living-off-the-land binaries.
- **Detection and Investigation (Walk)**: Expands into host forensics, disk and memory analysis, log triage, and implementing dedicated collection tools such as Velociraptor. Analysts learn to operationalize detection rules (YARA, Sigma) and perform initial malware triage.
- **Offensive Emulation and Specialization (Run)**: Analysts operate command-and-control (C2) frameworks and ransomware simulators to see attacks from the red-team perspective. Capabilities mature into cloud incident response, threat intelligence operationalization, purple teaming, and simulated cyber-range exercises.

### Takeaways
Effective workforce enablement relies on active, hands-on learning rather than passive listening. Practicing and operationalizing skills in lab environments drives substantially higher knowledge retention. By establishing structured onboarding, guided career roadmaps, and frequent practical workshops, organizations empower analysts to maximize existing tool investments, adapt to evolving attacker tactics, and dramatically boost operational resilience.

talks.title: Threat Hunting with a Chorus of Strings | Jonathan Ham
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Threat Hunting with a Chorus of Strings | Jonathan Ham.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Wild West Hackin' Fest in Deadwood, speaker Jonathan Ham explores low-fidelity network threat hunting under extreme operational constraints. Presenting a scenario where legacy packet captures (collected via WinPcap/WinDump) cannot be parsed by modern libpcap-based tools, Wireshark, or TCPDump, Ham sets out to prove that meaningful threat detection can still be achieved using nothing but the basic Unix utility `strings` against raw binary packet capture files.

### Key Topics
The talk centers on detecting three distinct cyber attack scenarios using only `strings` without protocol reconstruction or packet disassembly:
- **Watering Hole Attack & Portable Executable (PE) Identification:** Spotting cleartext HTTP traffic, file download artifacts, and dynamically linked libraries (DLLs) indicative of an executable transfer.
- **ICMP-Based Data Exfiltration:** Recognizing non-standard, obfuscated, and base64-encoded payloads transmitted within ICMP Echo Request packets.
- **DNS C2 Tunneling (iodine):** Hunting IP-over-DNS tunneling through character length profiling, 8-bit ASCII analysis, and identifying abnormal query names.

### Technical Details
- **Scenario 1: Watering Hole & PE Detection:** Ham runs `strings -n 12` (filtering for sequences of at least 12 printable ASCII characters) and pipes output to `less`, using regex matching for HTTP `GET` and `Host` headers. The investigation reveals requests to `lab.jhamcorp.com`, retrieving assets and ultimately `notepad.exe`. Grepping for `.dll` strings confirms the payload is a Portable Executable. Inspection of sequential strings reveals server responses with `Content-Type: application/x-msdos-program` and file size metadata. Ham highlights an anti-malware evasion trick where the standard compiler string `This program cannot be run in DOS mode` was altered using a hex editor to evade basic string-matching heuristic detections while keeping the executable functional.

- **Scenario 2: ICMP Data Exfiltration:** Outbound ICMP is often permitted enterprise-wide despite regular users having no business need to ping external resources. Ham demonstrates how data exfiltration tools (such as `hping3`) chunk stolen files into small payloads (e.g., 200 bytes) to avoid triggering legacy Snort rules for oversized ICMP payloads (rules frequently disabled due to MTU path discovery false positives). Even when an attacker compresses (gzip) and base64-encodes the data before transmission, running `strings -n 12` on the packet capture immediately exposes unnatural, repetitive, non-standard text blocks in the ICMP payload space, confirming anomalous activity.

- **Scenario 3: DNS Tunneling via iodine:** The `iodine` tool tunnels arbitrary IP traffic over DNS by gzipping packets and encoding them (using base32, base64, or base128) into DNS query names, typically utilizing NULL, TXT, or private resource records. Normal network traffic rarely exhibits long printable domain names (typically under 30 characters). Ham analyzes internal vs. external tunnel captures using `strings` with 7-bit ASCII and 8-bit encoding (`-e S`). While standard traffic contained zero strings longer than 60 characters, the base128-encoded DNS tunnel traffic yielded thousands of strings exceeding 20, 40, 80, 100, and even 200 characters in length. Recurring domain patterns (`giveyouup.jhamcorp.com`) allowed the discovery of the C2 tunnel endpoint.

### Takeaways
While relying solely on `strings` hides transport-layer metadata, source/destination IPs, ports, and protocols, it is sufficient to prove anomalous network behavior and validate hypotheses of malicious activity. Ham emphasizes that any system compromise will fundamentally alter its network and host behavior. When standard tools fail, primitive utilities can provide sufficient indicators to direct deeper file system and host-based forensic investigations. Ham also notes benchmarking findings that `ngrep` parses packets an order of magnitude faster than piping raw `strings` to `grep`.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at WWHF 2023, Christian Villapando shares guidance on how aspiring security professionals can break into the field and secure their first penetration testing gig. Speaking remotely from Manila, Villapando draws from his background as a pentest consultant for a US-based Fortune 100 company, master's student at the SANS Technology Institute, member of the Philippine CTF team Hacktivate, and advocate providing free cybersecurity training. He emphasizes that breaking into pentesting is achievable regardless of one's current age or background, provided one focuses on foundational skills, hands-on practice, and active community involvement.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Penetration Testing**: Villapando defines pentesting as an authorized attempt to access computer systems to improve an organization's security posture by identifying attack paths before malicious actors do. He clarifies that pentests are point-in-time assessments.
- **The Reality of Daily Pentesting Work**: Contrary to popular media portrayals of non-stop hacking, a pentester spends considerable time on non-hacking activities. These include client communication, scope definition, troubleshooting connectivity issues, writing reports as testing progresses, and providing post-delivery support and presentations.
- **Career Paths**: Aspiring professionals can enter the industry as full-time employees (at pentesting service firms or internal enterprise security teams), contractors paid by the hour for set durations (such as 3–6 months), or independent consultants running their own business, which provides more autonomy but relies heavily on industry reputation.
- **Types of Assessments**: Common assessments include web applications, external network testing, internal active directory assessments, wireless testing, mobile pentesting, and product or IoT embedded device testing. Web application testing is highlighted as the most common engagement and the usual entry point for beginners.
- **Core Fundamentals & Prerequisites**: Success requires solid grounding in computer networking (understanding concepts like TCP and the three-way handshake), operating systems (especially proficiency in Linux over standard Windows interfaces), and scripting or application development languages (recommending Python for scripting, alongside exposure to languages like PHP or Java). Those transitioning from other IT or infosec roles should also familiarize themselves with broader concepts like security controls, red and blue teams, and incident response.

### Technical Details & Learning Strategies
- **Training Platforms**: Villapando advocates leveraging free and paid learning resources, mentioning PortSwigger Web Security Academy for web application security, Hack The Box, TryHackMe, and material from SANS and OffSec.
- **Certifications**: While industry figures like Dave Kennedy and John Strand no longer need certifications due to their established reputations, certifications can help beginners pass initial HR screenings to land their first interview, though they are not an absolute requirement.
- **Goal Setting**: To maintain consistent progress, learners should set structured goals: daily goals (learning two current infosec news items or exploits), weekly goals (studying technical fundamentals like TCP RFCs), monthly goals (participating in a CTF), and quarterly or yearly goals (completing an online course or passing an exam).
- **Documentation and CTFs**: Writing public write-ups (e.g., documenting vulnerable machines on platforms like Medium) helps build communication skills and document personal growth. Hands-on CTF participation (such as competing in the DEF CON Red Team Village CTF) reinforces technical skills under realistic scenarios.

### Takeaways
To land a first pentesting role, candidates should focus heavily on troubleshooting fundamentals, gain hands-on practice via CTFs and labs, document their progress, and network within the community. For those already in IT or infosec, volunteering for dirty work, vulnerability assessments, or internal testing tasks can provide crucial visibility and experience. Pentesting ultimately balances technical hacking with communicating business risk to clients.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Wild West Hackin' Fest (WWHF) 2023, Gerard Johansen from Red Canary discusses how organizations can break down silos between red teams (offensive testers) and blue teams (incident response/defenders) to drastically improve incident response (IR) capabilities. Johansen argues that traditional security models treat penetration testing as an annual compliance checkbox exercise that leaves immense technical expertise on the table. Instead of jumping directly into complex, expensive annual purple team exercises where teams often fail, he advocates for a structured, year-round continuous training pipeline centered on realistic threat emulation.

### Key Topics
- **Silos and Checkbox Compliance:** Many organizations view security testing through a governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) lens, tightly scoping annual penetration tests to minor vulnerability scans or running Responder. This fails to provide actionable value or prepare defenders for real adversary behaviors.
- **The IR Training Gap:** Incident response training is frequently limited to annual tabletop exercises or costly multi-day offsite boot camps. Because budgets often get cut first in soft markets and technical skills degrade rapidly over months, defenders lack exposure to live adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
- **The "4 Rs" of Training:** Johansen asserts effective IR training must be Realistic (emulating genuine adversary behavior), Relevant (drawing from real threat intelligence like Red Canary's Threat Detection Report or Mandiant M-Trends), Recent (regularly practiced because training decays quickly), and Repetitive (drilled continuously rather than once a year).

### Technical Details & Framework
Johansen outlines a progressive, year-long training framework combining offensive and defensive capabilities:
- **IR Plan Review & Premortem Analysis (1-hour drill):** Engage red team personnel to review incident response and disaster recovery plans, conducting premortem analyses to spot assumptions adversaries could break (e.g., discovering online flat-file backup data lakes that an attacker could easily encrypt).
- **Monthly Detection & Response Micro-Emulations:** Conduct focused, single-technique emulations rather than entire kill chains using tools like Atomic Red Team or Caldera. Examples include testing `rundll32.exe` execution, DLL search order hijacking, LSASS memory dumping, or testing readiness against frameworks like Impacket, Cobalt Strike, or PowerShell Empire.
- **Tabletop Drills & Key Assumptions Checks:** Link discrete micro-emulations into partial kill chains (e.g., executing lateral movement via RDP, SMB, or GoToMyPC, and validating if defenders can locate Event ID 4624 Type 10 logon events and NetFlow artifacts within 10 minutes). Red teams participate in tabletops to challenge flawed managerial assumptions (e.g., proving whether an attacker can eavesdrop on incident response Zoom/WebEx channels).
- **Annual Purple Team Validation:** Conduct a full purple team engagement at the end of the year to validate cumulative progress across patched detective controls, playbook adjustments, and triage response speed.

### Takeaways
- **Continuous Tempo Outweighs Annual Splurges:** Organizations gain far more defensive resilience from continuous, low-cost weekly or monthly micro-emulations than from an isolated annual penetration test.
- **Actionable Metrics for Leadership:** Track technique-level metrics (e.g., mapping results on a MITRE ATT&CK spreadsheet) focusing on detection rate and dwell time/time-to-detect (e.g., flagging tests where activity was undetected after 90 minutes).
- **Mutual Benefits:** Red and blue cross-collaboration exposes defenders to the live attacker mindset and tooling while teaching red teams defensive detection boundaries and EDR telemetry evasion.

talks.title: Tool Demo - Riverside | Kaitlyn DeValk | WWHF Deadwood 2022

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk at WWHF Deadwood 2022, Kaitlyn DeValk presents Riverside, an open-source network security visualization tool she began developing during her Master's in Computer Science at the University of Maryland. Drawing from her background as a U.S. Coast Guard officer conducting penetration testing, vulnerability assessments, and red teaming at Coast Guard Cyber Command, DeValk discusses the persistent challenge of outdated, static network maps and the lack of accessible visualization tools outside expensive commercial software. Riverside was created as a proof-of-concept to offer real-time and historical network visibility through an interactive graphical interface.

### Key Topics
- **User-Informed Interface Design**: DeValk conducted interviews with network administrators and security analysts to understand user preferences, gathering feedback on diagram layouts (node-link diagrams, hierarchical views, and tabular formats).
- **Architecture and Data Ingestion**: The system relies on standalone Golang agents running packet capture via Berkeley Packet Filters (BPF) and deep packet inspection (DPI) to extract netflow data. Data is forwarded via gRPC to a Golang server, stored in PostgreSQL, and communicated to a JavaScript front end via WebSockets.
- **Interactive Temporal Visualization**: A dynamic timeline tracks real-time traffic while allowing users to scrub backward to inspect historical network states.
- **Visual Encoding and Customization**: Network nodes and edges visually reflect operational metadata, including protocol-based edge coloring, communication duration, frequency-based node transparency, and analyst customization.

### Technical Details
- **Backend & Communication**: Both the agents and the central server are written in Go. Agents capture network traffic similarly to tcpdump, requiring elevated permissions, and communicate with the server over gRPC (tested locally on port 1533). Configurations are handled via YAML files. The server uses the Gin framework for API and session management, while an ORM facilitates database management with PostgreSQL (deployed via Docker). Data models include tables for hosts (agents), remote hosts, and netflow records.
- **Packet Inspection**: The agent uses the `go-dpi` library for deep packet inspection to classify protocols (tracking roughly 12 protocols, such as DNS colored purple, SSL/HTTPS colored green, SMB, FTP, and RDP, falling back to gray/unknown if unclassified).
- **Visual Representation**: Agent nodes are differentiated from remote nodes (which default to gray). Edges show directionality (single or double-sided arrows) and throughput. Edges widen as continuous communication persists. Nodes incorporate a transparency mechanic where frequently communicating hosts fade, making rarer or newer connections stand out. Users can modify node labels, shapes, and colors during incident triage.
- **Compatibility**: Agents were tested across operating systems including Windows 10, Windows 11, Linux (Ubuntu, Kali, Pop!_OS), and within virtual machine environments.

### Takeaways & Future Work
Riverside is presented as a supportive tool to augment network visibility rather than a complete replacement for security toolsets. While the backend and binaries were released on GitHub, planned enhancements include front-end data filtering, visual timeline stamping for investigator actions, automated clustering for network segmentation, integration with external threat intelligence APIs (such as GreyNoise), and testing at larger enterprise network scales.

talks.title: A case for threat informed penetration testing | Dan DeCloss | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding A case for threat informed penetration testing | Dan DeCloss | WWHF Deadwood 2022.
talks.summary:
Dan DeCloss presents a business case for integrating threat intelligence with penetration testing programs to shift organizations from reactive to proactive security postures. He begins by establishing that traditional penetration testing and threat intelligence functions, while valuable, operate largely independently and sub-optimally.

Traditional Limitations: Standard penetration testing engagements typically occur infrequently (often annually), are broadly scoped, and apply baseline methodologies uniformly across engagements. While comprehensive, these generate voluminous findings and multiple attack paths, overwhelming blue teams with prioritization decisions. Reports can feel overwhelming, leaving defenders unsure where to begin remediation. Meanwhile, threat intelligence remains largely reactive—teams ingest threat feeds, extract indicators of compromise (IOCs), and push them into detection systems (SIEMs, firewalls) to identify known threats post-discovery. This keeps organizations in a responsive posture. Additionally, collaboration between red and blue teams is typically limited, as consulting firms move to next engagements or internal teams work in isolation.

The Core Problem: DeCloss frames the mission as making organizations and the world safer, identifying security gaps, and demonstrating measurable improvement. Traditional approaches leave teams fatigued by alerts, struggling to prioritize, and unable to articulate security progress to executives.

Threat-Informed Approach: The solution involves merging threat intelligence with continuous, iterative penetration testing. Rather than relying solely on annual assessments, organizations break testing into small, recurring cycles—for example, every two weeks. This approach applies threat intelligence to scope pen testing engagements, identifies actual threats relevant to the organization, and emphasizes context: understanding how a specific threat would execute in that environment, considering business model, compensating controls, and industry factors. Collaboration between red teams, blue teams, and threat intelligence teams (purple teaming) ensures all disciplines inform test plans and interpret results together. Agreed metrics measure progress over time, demonstrating trends in detection and defense capabilities.

Continuous Testing Model: Rather than eliminating annual assessments, the approach layers continuous testing atop them. When urgent intelligence emerges (e.g., Uber MFA fatigue breach), teams rapidly develop test plans. Otherwise, threat intelligence feeds into a backlog of known threats to iteratively test. This produces what DeCloss terms "fight while we train while we fight while we train"—constant readiness through ongoing validation.

Case Study: An anonymous large organization conducts weekly purple team exercises incorporating threat intelligence feeds. When the Uber breach surfaced, they quickly developed a test plan, validated controls with the blue team, identified gaps, and remediated—then communicated concrete findings to their board, replacing vague assurances with demonstrable actions. This improved board confidence and team morale.

Context as Critical: DeCloss emphasizes that applying threat context is paramount. Threat intelligence on specific threat actors or ransomware variants means nothing unless teams ask: How would this threat execute in our environment? Do these TTPs apply to us? What would success look like for an attacker here? This mirrors vulnerability management—a severity rating means nothing without understanding asset importance and compensating controls.

Measurement and Culture: By measuring outcomes against specific threats, teams show demonstrable progress, combat alert fatigue, and justify investments in tooling or personnel. Research shows purple teams adopting this approach report better morale, clearer understanding of true gaps, and stronger business cases for resources.

Key Takeaways: Adopt a programmatic approach with continuous, iterative testing and metrics. Integrate threat intelligence to drive test scope, not just reactive alerting. Build purple teams merging red, blue, and threat intelligence functions. Apply threat context to understand relevance before testing. Maintain annual/broader assessments for compliance and other attack paths. Measure and celebrate wins to demonstrate value and prevent fatigue. Move the majority of effort from reactive firefighting to proactive validation of known threats.

talks.title: Sustainable Phisheries: Preventing Disease in Farm Raised Phishing | Ean Meyer | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Sustainable Phisheries: Preventing Disease in Farm Raised Phishing | Ean Meyer | WWHF San Diego 2022.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Ian Meyer, Associate Director of Security Assurance at Marriott Vacations Worldwide and instructor at Full Sail University, discusses how to conduct phishing exercises in ways that preserve employee trust and organizational relationships rather than shaming users.

## The Fishing Metaphor and Core Problem
Meyer frames the issue as a "fishing industrial complex" where security vendors make it easy to conduct massive phishing campaigns that shame users. Like industrial fishing with nets that devastates fish populations, poorly designed phishing exercises deplete organizational trust. Meyer emphasizes that while phishing is easy to execute (like casting a wide net), sustainable security requires treating employees as valuable resources, not targets.

## Key Technical and Ethical Points

**Bad Practices:**
Meyer criticizes real examples where companies sent deceptive emails during the pandemic—GoDaddy teasing employees with fake holiday bonuses and Tribune Media offering false hardship assistance—to test if they'd click. These exercises violated psychological safety and used fear-based manipulation.

**The Scalpel Metaphor:**
Meyer uses a surgical scalpel as a metaphor for offensive security tools. A surgeon uses it to heal; an amateur kills. Security teams must think about downstream consequences before deploying phishing tests.

**Building Better Pretexts:**
Instead of fear-based messaging, Meyer demonstrates creating contextual, honest emails that match actual job duties. In a live audience example, he shows how shipping/logistics teams could receive emails about manifest updates (framed neutrally) and banking teams could receive customer inquiry emails—both based on real work patterns, not manipulation.

## Trust and Relationship Building

Meyer stresses that if security teams break trust through shame or punishment, employees stop reporting incidents. He shares a story of an employee who was fired after a social engineering exercise, despite leadership promising "nothing punitive." Result: help desk staff stopped talking to security, losing the organization's best source of threat intelligence.

Meyer demonstrates this through an audience participation exercise, throwing a trinket on a string into the crowd. When asked why the person opened the envelope, the answer was "trust"—the speaker wouldn't put something harmful in it. This trust is what security needs to build.

## Sustainable Security Program Model

Meyer advocates for:
- Removing shame-based language ("you have been fished")
- Using surveys asking *why* people clicked, not punishing them
- Recognizing anyone can be fished under the right circumstances
- Framing security team as enablers, not gatekeepers ("team of yes")
- Making employees security champions through partnership, not enforcement
- Focusing metrics on phishing *reporting* rates, not click rates

One of Meyer's exercises achieved 100% participation rate in a security champions program because employees felt respected and trusted.

## Actionable Takeaways

- Phishing exercises should emulate real threats but not use FUD (fear, uncertainty, doubt)
- Write pretexts aligned with employees' actual job duties
- Ask for help rather than testing obedience
- Partner with business units to gather feedback on controls gaps
- Meyer created a GitHub repository for crowd-sourced ethical phishing pretexts and landing pages
- Success metrics should track reporting and security champion engagement, not shame-based click rates

## Philosophy
Meyer concludes that security is about decreasing risk, not eliminating it. Businesses exist to take calculated risks. Security's job is to enable business while protecting against defined threats—this requires employee trust above all.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This hands-on workshop, presented by Bill Stearns alongside contributors from Black Hills Information Security and Active Countermeasures, provides an introductory yet practical guide to navigating, managing, and securing Linux systems via the command line. Designed as a safe learning environment, the session walks participants through foundational administration tasks, remote access setup, essential shell commands, system inspection, file navigation, and secure remote operations using SSH.

### Key Topics
- **Initial System Setup and Package Management:** Connecting to Linux instances (cloud VMs such as DigitalOcean, local VMs, or physical hosts), immediately resetting root passwords to prevent brute-force attacks, testing network/DNS reachability, using `apt update` and `apt full-upgrade`, and managing administrative rights via `sudo`.
- **Command Line Essentials & Process Management:** Viewing running processes using tree/forest views (`ps axf`), managing long outputs using the `less` pager, filtering strings with `grep`, capturing errors/stdout redirection (`2>&1`), and editing configuration files with `nano`.
- **System Hardware & Storage Inspection:** Querying hardware characteristics with `lshw`, reviewing block storage devices and partitions using `lsblk`, checking mounted file systems with `df -h` and `mount`, and distinguishing between physical filesystems (ext4) and virtual/kernel pseudo-filesystems (`/proc`, `/sys`, `tmpfs`).
- **Network Configuration & Monitoring:** Evaluating network interfaces with `ifconfig` and modern `ip addr` commands, inspecting routes via `route -n` and `ip route`, determining public IP addresses using simple HTTP queries via `netcat`, and tracking live performance metrics with tools like `top`, `atop`, and `gkrrelm`.
- **Filesystem Navigation & Remote Operations:** Navigating paths, utilizing the File System Hierarchy Standard (FHS), leveraging text-based file managers like Midnight Commander (`mc`), transferring files securely over the network with `scp`, and configuring passwordless authentication with SSH keys.

### Technical Details
- **User & Privilege Configuration:** Stearns emphasizes avoiding daily administrative operations as the root user. Instead, administrators should create non-root user accounts (e.g., via `useradd -m -G sudo labuser` or `adduser`), manage passwords with `passwd`, and utilize `sudo` for elevated tasks.
- **Process & Text Manipulation:** Running `ps axf | less -s` enables horizontal and vertical scrolling across process trees without wrapping. Stearns shows how chaining pipes—such as `sudo ps axf | grep nginx | grep -v grep`—isolates targeted daemon processes, while standard output and standard error redirection can be combined into files using `> file.txt 2>&1`.
- **Network Discovery & Verification:** Verifying ICMP and DNS connectivity is demonstrated via `ping -c 5 -n 8.8.8.8` and pinging hostnames. Stearns demonstrates raw socket HTTP interaction by echoing `GET /` into `nc icanhazip.com 80` to retrieve an outbound public IP address from NAT/virtual environments.
- **Remote File Management & SSH Hardening:** File transfers across hosts are executed using `scp [source] [destination]`. For SSH access (`sshd` on port 22), Stearns explains troubleshooting connection handshakes with `ssh -v`, and replacing standard password-based authentication by generating RSA key pairs (`id_rsa` and `id_rsa.pub` at 3072 bits) inside permissions-restricted directories (`chmod 700 ~/.ssh`).

### Takeaways
Command-line administration relies heavily on understanding core diagnostic tools, standard file locations, and secure administration habits. Stearns stresses avoiding root logins, inspecting system performance bottlenecks using granular tools like `atop`, moving data via encrypted SSH channels, and using accessible tools like `nano` and Midnight Commander to comfortably manage remote Linux infrastructure.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Wild West Hackin' Fest webcast, Bill Stearns (Active Countermeasures and Black Hills Information Security) presents a comprehensive guide on how to prepare and deliver effective technical presentations. Drawing on more than twenty years of industry and training experience, Stearns emphasizes that the primary goal of a technical talk is not merely reciting commands or facts, but motivating the audience and conveying genuine enthusiasm for the topic. The session offers practical advice spanning preparation logistics, slide design, vocal delivery, hands-on lab development, handling stage fright, and interacting with attendees.

### Key Topics
- **Audience Understanding and Topic Scope**: Selecting a topic requires understanding the specific audience background and experience level. As demonstrated by the "cooking chicken" exercise, a general topic cannot be developed effectively without knowing the audience's preexisting knowledge and interests.
- **Preparation and Logistical Redundancy**: Presenters must arrive early to test equipment and audio-visual setups. Stearns strongly advocates for hardware redundancy, advising speakers to carry multiple laptops, backup presentation remotes, spare batteries, display converters (DVI, HDMI, VGA), and backup internet access like cellular Wi-Fi pucks. Presentation files should exist on the laptop, online, and on a USB thumb drive kept in pocket.
- **Slide Design and Pacing**: Slides should feature high-contrast formatting (dark text on light backgrounds) and readable fonts. Speakers should use concise phrases or visual cues rather than full scripts to avoid sounding robotic. A baseline pacing rule of approximately two minutes per slide is recommended, along with reserving 15% to 25% of time for questions.
- **Overcoming Nervousness and Filler Words**: Rather than addressing a crowd collectively, speakers should treat presentations as a sequence of one-on-one conversations. To eliminate filler words, Stearns suggests practicing with an assistant who drops dollar coins into a glass jar whenever a filler is spoken.
- **Hands-On Lab Design**: Technical labs should prioritize the "light bulb moment" over laborious setup. Stearns outlines a three-tier lab structure comprising a basic goal description, optional hints, and explicit step-by-step commands. Using packaged cross-platform software or preconfigured cloud VMs is encouraged over requiring students to compile source code.

### Technical Details & Speaker Equipment
Stearns shares his specific setup and recommendations for virtual and in-person speaking:
- Hardware: Razer webcam, Blue Yeti microphone, in-ear monitor, and dedicated LED lights to properly illuminate darker spaces.
- Live Setup: Presentation remotes (such as Keyspan or Targus) with separate high-powered AAA laser pointers, avoiding low-power built-in watch battery pointers.
- Power and Travel: Verifying multi-voltage compatibility (110–240V, 50/60Hz) and bringing appropriate plug adapters for international events.

### Takeaways
- **Practice and Validation**: Rehearse presentations end-to-end with a timer. Record short video segments to review audio and video independently before combining them. Validate technical slides and lab walkthroughs with peer reviewers on fresh systems.
- **Humility and Authenticity**: It is critical to admit when you do not know an answer rather than fabricating explanations, followed by researching the answer and delivering it later.
- **Audience Connection**: Ditch protective physical barriers like podiums. Engage attendees visually, adjust the technical depth based on audience feedback, and provide persistent discussion channels (such as Discord) for continuous learning.

talks.summary:
## Overview
Kevin Johnson, CEO of Secure Ideas, presents 'Labours of Hercules—Be Like Phil,' using Disney's Hercules movie and its mentor character Phil as a framework for addressing the cybersecurity industry's real problems: not a talent shortage, but high training costs, unclear career paths, misinformation, and inadequate ethics education. Johnson advocates reframing cybersecurity as a skilled trade with formal mentorship pathways rather than an exclusive high-level profession.

## Key Problems Identified
Johnson highlights critical barriers: (1) training costs of $6,000–$7,000+ per course exclude many learners; (2) people lack understanding of career progression and where to focus learning; (3) incorrect technical information spreads online (citing a YouTube 'next-gen hacker 101' video that misinterprets traceroute output); (4) ethical and legal boundaries of security work aren't consistently taught—he describes a company scanning internet hosts without permission and questions how to teach people when and when not to apply penetration testing skills.

## The Apprentice-Journeyman-Mentor Model
Johnson proposes a three-stage progression: Apprentice (entry-level with defined foundational skills), Journeyman (competent practitioner capable of leading projects and consulting), and Mentor (guide for the next generation). Mentorship is bidirectional; mentors learn from mentees, and everyone at every level should mentor others. Johnson explicitly rejects the term 'master' due to negative connotations, emphasizing instead that reaching mentor status is only the beginning of responsibility, not an endpoint.

## Building Formal Mentorship Programs
Johnson outlines five implementation steps:

1. **Formalize the program:** Define goals, structure, communication plan, and schedule before launch. Clearly communicate expectations to all participants. Avoid ad-hoc mentoring ('we'll figure it out when we have time').

2. **Identify mentors actively:** Don't post open calls; actively recruit and engage potential mentors. Drag them into the program and work with them on adjusting plans.

3. **Provide multiple learning paths:** People learn differently. Some learn through reading, others via video, audio podcasts, hands-on practice, or group discussion. Secure Ideas uses written materials, recorded videos, live webcasts, Slack workspaces, and consultants available for real-time questions.

4. **Set clear SLAs:** Establish and communicate response time expectations (e.g., 30-minute response time during business hours). This is critical because mentees feel hesitant to ask questions and need assurance they won't be ignored.

5. **Ensure active engagement:** Reach out to all participants regularly. Track progress through assignments, quizzes, and practice exams. Pay attention to subtle feedback—if mentees say 'you haven't checked on me in weeks,' you're failing. When students say 'yeah yeah, I got it' without genuine understanding, probe deeper.

## Example Programs
Secure Ideas offers a CISSP mentorship program structured as recurring 9-week cycles with fixed start and end dates. Students can retake the program multiple times. Between cycles, previous participants naturally become mentors to new cohorts, creating sustainable community growth. Additionally, Johnson released Professional Evil Fundamentals—a free YouTube playlist of 2–4 minute definition videos covering foundational concepts.

## Guiding Philosophy
Johnson emphasizes that security professionals' primary responsibility is knowledge-sharing. He draws parallels to woodworking YouTubers like Steve Ramsey, who share crafts with genuine passion. Key principles:
- Everyone needs a mentor or hero; no one succeeds alone.
- Don't pursue applause or recognition; do the work because it matters.
- Follow ethical and legal rules; this distinguishes practitioners from those they oppose.
- Develop agility and broad competency, not isolated specialization.
- Aim with a flexible plan rather than rigid lists that guarantee imposter syndrome.

## Takeaways
The industry's real crisis is not talent shortage but accessibility and ethical education. Formalized, structured, bidirectional mentorship with multiple learning paths and active engagement prevents overwhelm and dropout. As practitioners gain expertise, mentoring the next generation becomes their primary responsibility.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, the speaker explores stealthy post-exploitation reconnaissance techniques, cautioning offensive security professionals against noisy, default actions such as immediately running Nmap upon gaining a foothold. Grounded in a systems administration background, the speaker advocates for adopting a "packet economy" mindset—minimizing network packets and blending in with standard user behaviors to avoid alerting blue teams and anomaly detection systems.

### Key Topics
- **Packet Economy and Avoiding Noisy Scanning:** Why relying immediately on tools like Nmap, full port scans, or heavy VM installations gives away an attacker's presence, and why testing detection monitoring requires discreet behavior.
- **Mimicking Normal User Activity:** Understanding normal operational hours, system local time, and baseline tools so post-exploitation activity does not stand out as anomalous.
- **Passive Network and Host Discovery:** Utilizing existing host artifacts—such as DNS caches, ARP tables, and mounted remote file systems—to map architecture and vendors without transmitting excessive traffic.
- **Internal OSINT and Data Mining:** Extracting metadata from internal documents (using concepts behind tools like FOCA and PowerMeta) and hunting credentials across logs, shell histories, and scripts.
- **Cloud Post-Exploitation Hygiene:** Caution regarding cloud metadata endpoints and API logging, advocating for checking scripts and cron jobs before making direct API calls.
- **Purposeful Escalation of Noise:** Transitioning from stealthy reconnaissance to intentionally raising noise levels once objectives are met in order to test and improve defensive detection capabilities.

### Technical Details
- **Activity Baseline Analysis:** Checking local system time, update/application logs (e.g., yum, apt, crontabs), and authentication records to pinpoint manual user interaction versus automated cron tasks. Application logs also reveal server usage peaks.
- **Host Footprinting via Built-in State:** Reading DNS caches to discover hostnames and domain naming conventions. Querying ARP tables (`arp -a`) exposes MAC addresses, allowing identification of hardware vendors (e.g., Cisco, Juniper) or hypervisors like VMware to detect virtualized/sandbox environments without slinging packets.
- **Credential Harvesting Artifacts:** Examining developer/debug logs for leaked credentials or failed password entries typed into username fields (such as seasonal passwords like `summer2019!`), reviewing `.bash_history` for passwords or S3 bucket references, and inspecting unencrypted SSH keys, `known_hosts`, and SSH config aliases to map pivoting paths.
- **Mounted File Systems and Query Methods:** Exploiting remote mounts (NFS, SMB via `mount` or `/etc/fstab`) to inspect remote systems without triggering active network inspection. On Linux, tools like `netstat`, `lsof`, and `ss` query network state differently (`proc` filesystem vs. direct kernel system calls), providing different operational visibility.

### Takeaways
Covert reconnaissance centers on patience, gathering context before acting, and looking for "permission" within the environment before running commands like Windows `net` utilities or specialized offensive tools. Offensive operators should conserve network packets, leverage built-in OS artifacts to infer network architecture, and throttle file downloads or search scripts. Finally, after silently meeting objectives, operators should systematically ratchet up their noise profile to help defenders benchmark their monitoring and response controls.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Jeff (Yoda66) and Derek Banks from Black Hills Information Security deliver an introductory overview of Android mobile application penetration testing. The speakers discuss the Android security model, market share landscape, key architectural components, required tooling, and practical testing methodologies. The session culminates in a technical explanation and live demonstration showing how to disassemble, modify, back-door, recompile, and sign a legitimate Android application with an embedded Metasploit Meterpreter payload.

### Key Topics
- **Android Market Share and Risk Landscape**: Android commands over 80% worldwide market share, featuring an open ecosystem where users frequently run older operating system versions (such as Lollipop, Marshmallow, or Nougat). Risks include enterprise data stored in applications, insecure dependencies, cleartext credential storage, and malicious or modified side-loaded apps.
- **Testing Environment and Tooling**: Setting up a dedicated mobile testing workbench requires tools like Android Studio (with AVD), Genymotion (x86-based emulator with VirtualBox), real rooted hardware devices (such as Google/Motorola Nexus devices), Jadx/Jadx-GUI for decompilation, Drozer for inter-process communication assessments, apktool for smali disassembly, and Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) for automated static and dynamic analysis.
- **Testing Methodology**: Pen testing mobile apps encompasses reconnaissance, filesystem analysis, network communication interception, and code review. Common methodology references include the OWASP Mobile Top 10 and Josh Wright's mobile device report cards.
- **Inter-Process Communication and Intents**: Android apps communicate via intents and broadcast receivers. Improperly filtered intents or vulnerable upstream libraries can expose internal functionality—such as accidentally exposing debug logging containing sensitive session cookies to the system log (logcat).

### Technical Details
- **Filesystem and Storage Analysis**: Android applications install by default into `/data/data/<app-package-name>/`. Testers can use `adb pull` before and after authenticating or interacting with an app, then run a diff to identify insecure data storage, including cleartext credentials and session tokens.
- **Network Traffic Interception**: Web traffic can be proxied using Burp Suite by generating its CA certificate, pushing it via `adb` (e.g., to `/sdcard/Download`), and installing it into the device's trusted credentials. Full packet capture can also be conducted using a software AP combined with Wireshark, tcpdump, or Bro.
- **Intent Exploitation with Drozer**: By port-forwarding TCP port 31415 using `adb forward tcp:31415 tcp:31415`, testers connect a host Drozer console to an on-device Drozer agent to stimulate exported activities, broadcast receivers, and services.
- **Backdooring APKs**: Disassembling an APK with `apktool` produces smali assembly files and extracts the binary `AndroidManifest.xml`. Meterpreter stagers generated by Metasploit can be disassembled into smali, copied into the target app's package structure, and called inside `onCreate` in the main activity file. Jeff demonstrated his Python automation script (`Android_EmbedIT` on GitHub) which decompiles both APKs, parses the XML to find the main activity entry point, injects the stager call, randomizes directory paths to evade simple detection, merges permissions, reassembles the app, and signs it with a newly generated keystore before launching a live reverse TCP Meterpreter handler.

### Takeaways
Android's openness and decoupled components provide substantial attack surface, especially when apps accept uncontrolled intents or rely on third-party libraries. Manual checks via ADB, decompilers like Jadx, and tools like MobSF and Drozer allow testers to rapidly locate serious flaws such as cleartext storage, leaky log files, and tampering opportunities. Organizations and users must exercise caution with side-loading APKs outside official app stores, and developers should use practice targets like DIVA (Damn Insecure Vulnerable App) to learn secure coding and validation practices.

talks.summary:
## Overview
In this presentation, Stan Jeff Kawa and Tom introduce Wordsmith, an open-source tool designed to generate targeted wordlists and usernames using geolocation data. After observing in penetration testing engagements that users frequently incorporate local geographic and cultural references—such as sports teams, landmarks, cities, street names, and religious references—into their passwords, the presenters created Wordsmith to automate the collection and generation of location-specific dictionaries. The talk covers the evolution from version 1 to a ground-up modular rewrite in version 2, detailed data sources, tool architecture, CLI mechanics, and real-world penetration testing case studies.

## Key Topics
- **Geolocation-Based Wordlist and Username Generation:** Moving beyond generic dictionary lists to create focused wordlists based on specific countries, states, counties, or cities. Wordsmith also utilizes regional demographic data, such as US Census and Social Security Administration records, to generate plausible user account names for password spraying and enumeration.
- **Data Sources and Ingestion:** Leveraging diverse public resources including the CIA World Factbook (demographics, common languages, religions), OpenStreetMap (roads, cities, counties), Project Gutenberg (religious texts such as various editions of the Bible and Quran), Wikipedia (sports teams, universities, landmarks), and spellcheck dictionaries (Hunspell, LibreOffice/OpenOffice) for multilingual wordsets.
- **Architecture and Extensibility:** Version 2 organizes data into an ISO alpha-3 flat-file directory structure with YAML configuration files and modular text files per attribute, allowing community contributors to add local data sets easily without needing deep coding experience.

## Technical Details
- **CLI Usage and Boundary Selection:** Wordsmith (`wordsmith.rb`) accepts geographic boundaries (`-I`) ranging from entire continents and multi-country aliases defined in a `regions.csv` file, down to ISO country codes, state abbreviations, and specific municipalities. Attributes (`-a` for all, or dedicated flags like `-R` for roads, `-L` for landmarks, `-Z` for zip codes, and `-X` for miscellaneous custom files) define what terms are aggregated.
- **Mangling and Filtering Options:** Wordsmith provides flags to enforce minimum or maximum character lengths, perform basic mangling (such as removing punctuation and splitting strings), strip non-compliant strings matching standard password policy complexity rules (`-D` for Windows default complexity requiring 3 of 4 character sets and at least 8 characters), and prepend or append common patterns like area codes, zip codes, or custom year masks.
- **Username Generation and Kerb-Guessing:** Using the top 100 first and last names by location, Wordsmith can output common enterprise username permutations (`first.last`, `flast`, etc.). In a demonstrated Active Directory assessment, pre-authentication Kerberos requests ("kerb-guessing") against domain controllers allowed the tester to validate 505 active user accounts out of a generated list without triggering failed authentication lockouts, uncovering nearly half of the organization's valid user accounts.
- **Hash Cracking Results:** In an engagement demo targeting an Irish client, an 800,000-word geolocation-focused wordlist was generated in 12 seconds. Paired with Hashcat and the 50,000-rule `dead_hob0` mangling ruleset, it recovered 101 out of 533 unique NTLM hashes (approximately 20%) in roughly 80 seconds, uncovering local street addresses, landmarks, and regional surnames.

## Takeaways
- Targeted, location-aware wordlists significantly increase the efficiency and success rate of credential recovery and password spraying against regional and multinational organizations.
- Wordsmith version 2 offers a fully modular, community-driven structure across more than 230 countries and territories, supporting multilingual text and custom attributes.
- Future plans discussed for version 3 include radius-based wordlist generation via geographic coordinates, API development, and broader integration with OpenStreetMap and lyrics databases.
